Lecture 18

Convergence in probability, in mean and in distribution; the central limit theorem

Deck B, slides 20 to 30 · 51 min read · 30 practice problems

Solutions stay collapsed until you click them.

Where we are. In L17 we judged convergence one path at a time: fix ω, look at the sequence Xn​(ω). This lecture gives three modes that don't look at paths at all. Instead they look at probabilities or averages at each fixed n:

  • In probability: big mistakes become unlikely.
  • In r-th mean: the average size of the mistake goes to 0.
  • In distribution: only the CDFs converge. The values themselves don't have to get close.

Then all five modes go into one picture, and the lecture ends with the most important "in distribution" result of the whole course, the central limit theorem (CLT), plus how to actually use it (the normal approximation).

Part A: the slides

Slide 20/30: Towards convergence in probability

On the slide. Now define Xn​=n1{Un​≤n1​}​ where the {Un​} are i.i.d. uniform. Xn​=n when Un​≤n1​ and Xn​=0 otherwise. What can you say about {Xn​}? Is it true that once an Xn​ is zero, all higher-indexed variables are also zero? No! On every run of the experiment (every sample path), we will have a sequence of zero and non-zero values, where the non-zero values become rarer and rarer but keep happening once in a while. On no sample path would you see convergence to zero, but the occurrence of non-zero values becomes rare. We now characterise this notion of convergence.

This is L17 slide 19 with one change: U→Un​. Instead of one uniform shared by everyone, each n gets its own fresh, independent uniform. Each Xn​ on its own has exactly the same distribution as before (n with probability n1​, else 0). What changes is how they behave together.

Slide 19: one U Slide 20: independent Un​
A typical path 1,2,3,0,0,0,0,… 1,0,0,4,0,0,…,0,37,0,…,0,912,0,…
Once 0, always 0? yes (for u>0) no
a.s. convergence to 0? yes no
Distribution of each Xn​ n w.p. n1​ the same

Why the nonzero values never stop. This is how to make the slide's claim precise. The events En​={Un​≤n1​} are independent and ∑n​P(En​)=∑n1​=∞. So by the second Borel–Cantelli lemma (L17 slide 18), with probability 1, infinitely many of them happen. That means Xn​=n for infinitely many n, so the path doesn't go to 0. It's actually unbounded. (The slide's "on no sample path" should be read as "on a set of paths with probability 1".)

But they do get rare. The expected number of nonzero values among n=1001,…,106 is

n=1001∑106​n1​≈ln106−ln103=ln1000≈6.9.

So out of about a million terms, only around 7 are nonzero. For any single large n, Xn​ is almost certainly 0. That's exactly the property the next slide turns into a definition.

Slide 21/30: Convergence in probability

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X in probability if limn→∞​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0 for all ϵ>0. How would you compute P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ) when Xn​,X are continuous or discrete? Example: Xn​=n with probability n1​ and Xn​=0 otherwise. P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=P(Xn​>ϵ)=n1​ when n>ϵ. When n<ϵ, P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0. Once n>ϵ, limn→∞​P(Xn​>ϵ)=limn1​=0. Xn​ converges to 0 in probability, but not almost surely. a.s. convergence implies convergence in probability.

Xn​p​X⟺for every ϵ>0: n→∞lim​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0​

In words: pick any tolerance ϵ. The chance of being off by more than ϵ at time n goes to 0. The title's "w.h.p." means with high probability: for large n, Xn​ is within ϵ of X with probability close to 1.

Compare with L17: a.s. convergence wanted the mistakes to stop for good on almost every path. Here we only ask that at each single time n, a mistake is unlikely. Mistakes are allowed to keep popping up forever, as long as they get rarer.

How do you compute P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)? (the red question)

  • X is a constant c (this is the usual case). Then you only need the distribution of Xn​:
P(∣Xn​−c∣>ϵ)=P(Xn​<c−ϵ)+P(Xn​>c+ϵ).

That's a sum of pmf values (discrete) or the integral of the pdf outside [c−ϵ,c+ϵ] (continuous).

  • X is random. Now you need the distribution of the difference Dn​=Xn​−X, and for that you need the joint distribution of Xn​ and X. A common easy case: Xn​=X+Yn​, then Dn​=Yn​.
  • If computing it exactly is a pain, bound it with Markov or Chebyshev instead (the box after slide 22).

The slide's example. X=0 and ∣Xn​∣=Xn​∈{0,n}. For n>ϵ, P(Xn​>ϵ)=P(Xn​=n)=n1​→0. So Xn​p​0.

Notice this works for both slide 19's and slide 20's sequences. Convergence in probability only looks at the distribution of Xn​−X for each n separately, and those are the same in both cases. So it can't tell the two apart, but a.s. convergence can. That's exactly why "in probability" is the weaker one.

a.s. ⇒ in probability (proof). Fix ϵ and use Am​={∣Xn​−X∣<ϵ for all n≥m} from Theorem 7.6. If Xn​a.s.​X, then P(Am​)→1. Now, Am​ says "close at every time from m on", which in particular means "close at time m". So Am​⊆{∣Xm​−X∣<ϵ}, and

P(∣Xm​−X∣<ϵ)≥P(Am​)→1.

So P(∣Xm​−X∣≥ϵ)→0. □ (Bertsekas Problem 15.)

The converse is false, and slide 20 is the counterexample.

Slide 22/30: Convergence in r-th mean

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X in r-th mean if limn→∞​E[∣Xn​−X∣r]=0. How will you compute E[∣Xn​−X∣r]? When r=2 it is convergence in the mean-squared sense; in addition, if X=0, it implies that the second moments converge to 0. In the convergence in probability example, do we have convergence in mean or mean square? Convergence in r-th mean implies convergence in probability.

Xn​Lr​X⟺n→∞lim​E[∣Xn​−X∣r]=0​(r≥1)

Now we don't ask about the chance of a big mistake, we ask about the average size of the mistake (raised to the power r). r=1 is called convergence in mean, and r=2 is mean-square convergence, written Xn​m.s.​X.

How to compute E[∣Xn​−X∣r]. It's just LOTUS on the difference Dn​=Xn​−X:

E[∣Dn​∣r]=d∑​∣d∣rpDn​​(d)or∫∣d∣rfDn​​(d)dd.

Same as before: if X=c is a constant, you only need the law of Xn​.

For mean square with a constant limit there's a shortcut with no integrals at all, the bias–variance decomposition:

E[(Xn​−c)2]=Var(Xn​)+(E[Xn​]−c)2​

Why: write Xn​−c=(Xn​−E[Xn​])+(E[Xn​]−c) and square. The first piece squared averages to Var(Xn​), the second is a constant, and the cross term is 2(E[Xn​]−c)E[Xn​−E[Xn​]]=0.

So Xn​m.s.​c exactly when E[Xn​]→c and Var(Xn​)→0. In practice this is the fastest test there is.

The slide's question: does the example converge in mean? No.

E∣Xn​−0∣=n⋅n1​=1for every n,

which doesn't go to 0. Mean square is even worse: E[Xn2​]=n2⋅n1​=n→∞. So this example converges in probability but not in mean or mean square. Same reason as L17 slide 19: a rare but huge value.

Lr⇒ in probability (the red bullet). Use Markov's inequality (box below) on the nonnegative variable ∣Xn​−X∣r:

P(∣Xn​−X∣≥ϵ)=P(∣Xn​−X∣r≥ϵr)≤ϵrE∣Xn​−X∣r​→0.□

(probabilitycourse Theorem 7.4; last year's HW8 Q7 and Tutorial 7 Q9.)

Also, a higher mean is a stronger requirement: if s≥r≥1, then Ls convergence implies Lr convergence (probabilitycourse Theorem 7.3). In particular mean square ⇒ convergence in mean.

The sample mean converges in mean square. By L17 slide 15,

E[(μ^​n​−μ)2]=Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​→0.

So μ^​n​m.s.​μ, and therefore μ^​n​p​μ. That last statement is the weak law of large numbers, coming up next.

Toolkit box (Bertsekas 5.1 and 5.2): Markov, Chebyshev and the weak law

These aren't on this year's slides, but they're the standard way to prove convergence in probability, and last year's Tutorial 7 Q8 said to "use directly" these.

Markov's inequality. If X≥0 and a>0,

P(X≥a)≤aE[X]​​

Proof. The key observation is a1{X≥a}≤X, always. Check both cases: if X≥a, the left side is a, which is ≤X; if X<a, the left side is 0≤X. Now take expectations: aP(X≥a)≤E[X]. □

The intuition: a nonnegative variable with a small mean can't put much probability on big values, because those big values alone would already push the mean up.

Chebyshev's inequality. If X has mean μ and variance σ2, then for c>0,

P(∣X−μ∣≥c)≤c2σ2​​

Proof. ∣X−μ∣≥c is the same as (X−μ)2≥c2. Apply Markov to the nonnegative (X−μ)2 with a=c2:

P((X−μ)2≥c2)≤c2E[(X−μ)2]​=c2σ2​.

(This is last year's Tutorial 7 Q8(a).) □

How good are these bounds? (Bertsekas Ex. 5.1, 5.2.) Pretty crude.

  • X∼U[0,4]: Markov gives P(X≥3)≤32​, but the truth is 41​. Chebyshev gives P(∣X−2∣≥1)≤14/3​=34​, which says nothing at all (the truth is 21​).
  • X∼ Exp(1): Chebyshev gives P(X≥c)≤(c−1)21​, while the truth is e−c, way smaller.

They're useful anyway because they only need a mean (and a variance). That's perfect for proofs, where you usually don't know the full distribution.

The weak law of large numbers (WLLN). For i.i.d. Xi​ with mean μ and variance σ2, apply Chebyshev to μ^​n​ (mean μ, variance nσ2​):

P(∣μ^​n​−μ∣≥ϵ)≤nϵ2σ2​n→∞​0,soμ^​n​p​μ​

It's called "weak" because convergence in probability is weaker than the SLLN's almost sure convergence (and the SLLN implies it). What the WLLN has going for it: a one-line proof, and an explicit bound you can use for a finite n.

Example (Bertsekas 5.5). Mn​ is the average of n i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) variables, p unknown. Each has variance p(1−p)≤41​ (largest at p=21​). Chebyshev gives

P(∣Mn​−p∣≥ϵ)≤4nϵ21​.

How big must n be so that Mn​ is within 0.01 of p with probability at least 0.95? Need 4n(0.01)21​≤0.05, i.e. n≥50,000. (The CLT at the end of this lecture says 9604 is enough. Chebyshev is that crude.)

Slide 23/30: Weak convergence (in distribution)

On the slide. Xn​ converges to X in distribution if limn→∞​FXn​​(x)=FX​(x) for all continuity points of FX​(⋅). a.s. convergence and convergence in probability imply convergence in distribution. Example: Xn​ is exponential with parameter λn. Then FXn​​(x)=1−e−nλx and FX​(x)=1 for all x [≥0]. Note x=0 is a point of discontinuity, as FX​(0)=1 and FXn​​(0)=0. HW EX2: Xn​ are [independent] Binomial(n,nλ​). It converges in distribution to Poisson(λ).

Xn​d​X⟺FXn​​(x)→FX​(x) at every x where FX​ is continuous​

(Two small slips on the slide. "FX​(x)=1 for all x" should be "for all x≥0", since FX​(x)=0 for x<0. And the HW's "i.i.d." can't be literal, since the Xn​ have different distributions. It just means Xn​∼ Binomial(n,nλ​).)

What it says and what it doesn't. Only the CDFs get compared. The values Xn​(ω) never have to be close to X(ω). The variables don't even have to live on the same Ω.

For example, take X∼N(0,1) and Xn​=−X for all n. By symmetry FXn​​=FX​, so Xn​d​X trivially. But ∣Xn​−X∣=2∣X∣ never shrinks. That's why this mode is called weak convergence.

The slide's example: Exp(λn). The mean is λn1​→0, so we expect Xn​→0. The CDF of the constant X=0 is a step: FX​(x)=1{x≥0}. Check each x:

  • x<0: FXn​​(x)=0=FX​(x). ✓
  • x>0: FXn​​(x)=1−e−nλx→1=FX​(x). ✓
  • x=0: FXn​​(0)=0 for every n, but FX​(0)=1. ✗

So the CDFs converge everywhere except at the jump of FX​. If the definition demanded convergence at every single x, this totally obvious example would fail. That's the reason only continuity points count. (It's the L16 example 1−e−nx again, with its non-uniform convergence near 0.)

Why a.s. and in probability imply in distribution. The slide just states it. Here's the idea for "in probability ⇒ in distribution". Suppose Xn​≤x. Then either X≤x+ϵ, or X is more than ϵ away from Xn​. So

FXn​​(x)≤FX​(x+ϵ)+P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ),

and the same reasoning the other way gives

FX​(x−ϵ)−P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)≤FXn​​(x).

Let n→∞ (the probabilities go to 0), then ϵ→0. At a continuity point, FX​(x±ϵ)→FX​(x), so FXn​​(x) is squeezed to FX​(x). □

The converse does hold when the limit is a constant (last year's Tutorial 8 Q3). If Xn​d​c, then Xn​p​c. Proof. The limit CDF is the step 1{x≥c}, whose only jump is at c. So c−ϵ and c+ϵ are continuity points, and

P(∣Xn​−c∣>ϵ)≤FXn​​(c−ϵ)+1−FXn​​(c+ϵ)→0+1−1=0.□

For integer-valued variables, just compare pmfs (probabilitycourse Theorem 7.1). If all Xn​ and X take values in {0,1,2,…}, then

Xn​d​X⟺P(Xn​=k)→P(X=k) for every k.

For MGFs (the continuity theorem, Bertsekas uses it without proof). If MXn​​(s)→MX​(s) for all s in some interval around 0, then Xn​d​X. This is how the CLT gets proved.

HW EX2: Binomial(n,nλ​)d​ Poisson(λ), two proofs.

Proof 1 (pmfs, probabilitycourse 7.2.4 Example 3). Fix k and split the binomial pmf into pieces whose limits we know:

P(Xn​=k)=(kn​)(nλ​)k(1−nλ​)n−k=k!λk​⋅→1nkn(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)​​​⋅→e−λ(1−nλ​)n​​⋅→1(1−nλ​)−k​​ ⟶ k!e−λλk​.

The first underbrace is k factors each close to n, divided by nk. The last one has a fixed power k of something going to 1. By Theorem 7.1, Xn​d​ Poisson(λ).

Proof 2 (MGFs). The Bernoulli(p) MGF is 1−p+pet, so the binomial one is its n-th power. Using toolkit fact 9, (1+na​)n→ea:

MXn​​(t)=(1−nλ​+nλ​et)n=(1+nλ(et−1)​)n⟶eλ(et−1),

which is the Poisson(λ) MGF.

So: count the successes in lots of independent trials, each with a tiny success probability, keeping the expected count λ fixed, and you get a Poisson count.

Slide 24/30: Summary of the five modes

On the slide. A chart (from Wikipedia): pointwise convergence, limXn​(ω)=X(ω) for every ω; almost sure convergence, limXn​(ω)=X(ω) almost surely; convergence in probability, limP(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0 for any ϵ>0; mean-square convergence, limE[(Xn​−X)2]=0; convergence in distribution, limFn​(x)=F(x) for any continuity point x.

All five side by side:

Mode Definition What it looks at Quick test
Sure Xn​(ω)→X(ω) for all ω every path rarely used
Almost sure P(Xn​→X)=1 paths, ignoring probability 0 Borel–Cantelli: ∑n​P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)<∞; or Theorem 7.6; or monotone sequences
In probability P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)→0 one n at a time compute it, or Markov/Chebyshev
Mean square E[(Xn​−X)2]→0 one n at a time, on average E[Xn​]→c and Var(Xn​)→0 (constant c)
In distribution FXn​​(x)→FX​(x) at continuity points only the marginal CDFs CDFs, pmfs (integer case), or MGFs

Going down the table, each mode cares about less and less: from every path, to almost every path, to one time at a time, to just the shape of the distribution.

Slide 25/30: Relations between the modes (no proofs)

On the slide. Almost sure convergence ⇒ convergence in probability ⇐ mean-square convergence; convergence in probability ⇒ convergence in distribution. (Link: Wikipedia, proofs of convergence of random variables.)

sure⇒almost sure​↘​in probability⇓in distribution​↙​mean square (L2)⇒L1​

Every arrow is proved above: a.s. ⇒ p (slide 21), Lr⇒ p (slide 22), p ⇒ d (slide 23).

Now the arrows that are missing. Each one has a counterexample, and it's really worth memorising them, because exam questions like "does it converge in mode X? in mode Y?" are built out of exactly these.

Claim False because of Details
p ⇒ a.s. slide 20: Xn​=n1{Un​≤n1​}, independent Un​ ∑n1​=∞ plus independence: infinitely many nonzeros
p ⇒ m.s. (or L1) slide 21: Xn​=n w.p. n1​ E∣Xn​∣=1
a.s. ⇒ m.s. (or L1) slide 19: Xn​=n1{U≤n1​}, one U converges a.s., but E[Xn​]=1
m.s. ⇒ a.s. independent Xn​∼ Bernoulli(n1​) E[Xn2​]=n1​→0, but infinitely many 1s (L17 B4)
d ⇒ p X∼N(0,1), Xn​=−X; or i.i.d. copies of X same CDFs, values never close

And the one partial converse: d ⇒ p when the limit is a constant.

Notice the pattern: the "rare but huge value" examples break the mean modes, and the "independent, divergent sum" examples break a.s. convergence.

Slide 26/30: Towards the CLT

On the slide. Recall μ^​n​=nSn​​ where Sn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, and {Xi​} is i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2. E[μ^​n​]=μ and var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​. Now consider Yn​=σ/n​μ^​n​−μ​ (centering and scaling). What are the mean and variance of Yn​? E[Yn​]=0 and Var(Yn​)=1. What is FYn​​(⋅)? What is limn→∞​FYn​​(⋅)? Answer: Φ(⋅)=FN(0,1)​(⋅). In other words, Yn​ converges to Y=N(0,1) in distribution.

Standardising. Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation:

Yn​=σ/n​μ^​n​−μ​=σn​Sn​−nμ​.

(For the second form, multiply top and bottom by n.) Then

E[Yn​]=σ/n​E[μ^​n​]−μ​=0,Var(Yn​)=σ2/nVar(μ^​n​)​=1.

Why divide by exactly n​σ​? Look at Sn​−nμ and try dividing by different powers of n:

  • Divide by n: you get μ^​n​−μ→0 (LLN). Too much shrinking, the limit is just the constant 0. Nothing interesting left.
  • Don't divide at all: Var(Sn​−nμ)=nσ2→∞. It spreads out forever.
  • Divide by n​: the variance stays at σ2, and the shape settles down.

So n​ is the one scaling that "zooms in" on the fluctuations of μ^​n​ around μ at just the right rate to keep them visible. And the amazing part (next slide) is that the shape you see is always the same.

Slides 27/30 and 28/30: The central limit theorem

On the slide (27). Let {Xn​,n≥0} be i.i.d. random variables, each with mean μ and variance 0<σ2<∞. Let μ^​n​=n∑i=1n​Xi​​ and Yn​=σ/n​μ^​n​−μ​. Then Yn​ converges to N(0,1) in distribution. The Xi​ could be ANY discrete or continuous random variables with finite mean and variance. What is the consequence when E[Xi​]=0 and Var(Xi​)=1? Then Yn​=n​Sn​​, and it converges in distribution to N(0,1). nSn​​ converges almost surely to 0, but n​Sn​​ converges to a random variable N(0,1).

On the slide (28). (Same box.) The CLT gives a way to find the approximate distribution of μ^​n​. For large enough n, we can use the approximation Yn​∼N(0,1). Since Gaussianity is preserved under affine transformations, μ^​n​∼N(μ,nσ2​) [approximately].

σn​Sn​−nμ​d​N(0,1),that is,n→∞lim​P(σn​Sn​−nμ​≤z)=Φ(z) for every z​

(Φ is continuous everywhere, so here the CDFs converge at every z, no exceptions.)

What's so remarkable. The Xi​ can have any distribution with a finite variance: Bernoulli, uniform, exponential, a die, a mixture, whatever. In the limit the shape of that distribution is completely forgotten. Only μ and σ2 survive.

The blue question: E[Xi​]=0, Var(Xi​)=1. Then Yn​=n​Sn​​, and we can put the two laws side by side:

nSn​​a.s.​0  (SLLN),n​Sn​​d​N(0,1)  (CLT).

Dividing by n kills all the randomness. Dividing by n​ keeps exactly one unit of it. (Side note: n​Sn​​ does not converge in probability to anything. Only its distribution settles down.)

Slide 28, the practical version. For large n, pretend Yn​ is exactly N(0,1). Then undo the standardisation. Since an affine map of a normal is normal,

μ^​n​≈N(μ,nσ2​),Sn​≈N(nμ,nσ2)​

This finally answers L17 slide 15's question "what is the CDF of μ^​n​?", and you don't even need to know the distribution of the Xi​.

How large is "large enough"? The usual rule of thumb is n≥30. It works faster when the Xi​ are symmetric (a sum of just 12 uniforms is already very close to normal), and slower when they're skewed (Bernoulli with p near 0 or 1, exponential) or heavy-tailed.

Proof sketch via MGFs (Bertsekas Problem 12; L14 Part B, B13; last year's Tutorial 6 Q4). Assume the MGF exists near 0. Standardise each term: Zi​=σXi​−μ​, so E[Zi​]=0, E[Zi2​]=1, and Yn​=n​1​∑i=1n​Zi​.

  1. Independence turns the sum into a power (L14 slide 6, plus MaX​(s)=MX​(as)):
MYn​​(s)=E[en​s​∑Zi​]=i=1∏n​E[en​s​Zi​]=[MZ​(n​s​)]n.
  1. Taylor expand MZ​ near 0. We know MZ​(0)=1, MZ′​(0)=E[Z]=0, MZ′′​(0)=E[Z2]=1, so
MZ​(u)=1+2u2​+o(u2)⟹MZ​(n​s​)=1+2ns2​+o(n1​).
  1. Take the limit, using (1+na​+o(n1​))n→ea:
MYn​​(s)=[1+ns2/2​+o(n1​)]n→es2/2,

the MGF of N(0,1). 4. Conclude with the continuity theorem (slide 23): the MGFs converge to the N(0,1) MGF, so Yn​d​N(0,1). □

Notice where the n​ matters: it makes the u2 term exactly of size n1​, which is what gives a nontrivial limit after raising to the power n. With ns​ in place of n​s​ (i.e. looking at μ^​n​ itself), the same computation gives Mμ^​n​​(s)→esμ, the MGF of the constant μ. That's the WLLN (probabilitycourse 7.1.3 Problem 5). The fully general CLT (no MGF assumed) uses characteristic functions in exactly the same way.

Slide 29/30: Example from probabilitycourse.com

On the slide. Assumptions: X1​,X2​,… are i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) and Zn​=np(1−p)​X1​+⋯+Xn​−np​, with p=31​. Plots of the PMFs of Z1​,Z2​,Z3​ and Z30​.

Here μ=p=31​ and σ2=p(1−p)=92​. Sn​∼ Binomial(n,31​), and Zn​=2n/9​Sn​−n/3​ is just its standardised version. These are the numbers behind the plots:

n values of Zn​ probabilities
1 −0.707, 1.414 32​, 31​
2 −1, 0.5, 2 94​, 94​, 91​
3 −1.225, 0, 1.225, 2.449 278​, 2712​, 276​, 271​
30 2.582k−10​ for k=0,…,30, spaced 0.387 apart (k30​)(31​)k(32​)30−k

How to get a row, say n=2: S2​∈{0,1,2} with probabilities (32​)2,2⋅31​⋅32​,(31​)2, and Z2​=4/9​S2​−2/3​=2/3S2​−2/3​, which gives −1,0.5,2.

What the pictures show.

  • Every Zn​ has mean 0 and variance 1. That's by construction.
  • For small n the pmf is lopsided: a tall bar on the left and a long tail on the right, because p=31​<21​ makes the Bernoulli skewed.
  • By n=30 the bars trace out a bell curve. The skew fades like n​1​.
  • But the bars themselves keep getting shorter (each one is about 0.387×φ(z)), so the pmfs don't converge to anything. It's the CDFs that converge to Φ. That's why the CLT is stated as convergence in distribution. Equivalently: rescale the histogram to have area 1 (divide each bar's height by the spacing 0.387), and then it approaches the density φ.

Slide 30/30: The normal approximation based on the CLT

On the slide. Let Sn​=X1​+⋯+Xn​ where the Xi​ are i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2. If n is large, the CDF of Sn​ can be approximated as P(Sn​<c)≈Φ(z) where z=σn​c−nμ​. (Video link: youtube.com/watch?v=zeJD6dqJ5lo.)

P(Sn​≤c)≈Φ(σn​c−nμ​),P(μ^​n​≤c)≈Φ(σ/n​c−μ​)​

The recipe (probabilitycourse 7.1.2).

  1. Write the thing you care about as a sum Sn​ (or an average) of i.i.d. terms.
  2. Find μ=E[Xi​] and σ2=Var(Xi​). Then E[Sn​]=nμ and SD(Sn​)=σn​.
  3. Standardise the boundary: z=σn​c−nμ​.
  4. Read Φ(z) off the table. Use 1−Φ(z) for ">", Φ(z2​)−Φ(z1​) for an interval, and Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z) for negative z.

The continuity correction (De Moivre–Laplace). Here's the problem. If Sn​ only takes integer values (binomial, Poisson, counts), then P(Sn​<c), P(Sn​≤c) and P(Sn​≤c−1) can be genuinely different numbers. But plugging them into the normal approximation would give almost the same answer for all of them. The fix: put the boundary halfway between integers. For integers k≤l,

P(k≤Sn​≤l)≈Φ(σn​l+21​−nμ​)−Φ(σn​k−21​−nμ​).

The picture: think of each integer j as a histogram bar covering [j−21​,j+21​]. You're approximating the total area of the bars from k to l by the area under the normal curve over the same stretch, so the stretch has to go from k−21​ to l+21​.

Bertsekas Ex. 5.12. S∼ Binomial(36,21​): mean 18, SD 36⋅41​​=3.

  • Exact: P(S≤21)=0.8785.
  • No correction: Φ(321−18​)=Φ(1)=0.8413. Off by 0.04.
  • With correction: Φ(321.5−18​)=Φ(1.17)=0.8783. Off by 0.0002.
  • It even works for a single value: P(S=19)≈Φ(319.5−18​)−Φ(318.5−18​)=0.6915−0.5662=0.1253, against the exact (1936​)2−36=0.1251. (Without the correction you'd get Φ(31​)−Φ(31​)=0, which is nonsense.)

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

General plan. For "does Xn​ converge in probability / mean square / distribution?":

  • Constant limit, mean square: check E[Xn​]→c and Var(Xn​)→0. If yes, you also get in probability and in distribution for free.
  • In probability: compute P(∣Xn​−c∣>ϵ) directly, or bound it with Markov (needs a mean) or Chebyshev (needs a variance).
  • In distribution: compute the CDF and take the limit (ignore jump points of the limit), or compare pmfs for integer-valued variables, or use MGFs.
  • To show something fails: look for a rare huge value (kills the mean modes), or variables that keep the same distribution but stay apart (kills in probability).

Convergence in probability and in mean

B1 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.7). Y∼ Exp(1) and Yn​=nY​. (The Yn​ are dependent.) Does Yn​→0 in probability?

Solution

Solution. ∣Yn​∣≥ϵ means Y≥nϵ, so

P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)=P(Y≥nϵ)=e−nϵ→0.

Yes. Actually it's even sure convergence: Yn​(ω)=nY(ω)​→0 for every single outcome.

B2 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.8; probabilitycourse 7.2.6). Yn​=n2 with probability n1​, else 0. Show Yn​p​0 but E[Yn​]→∞, and no Lr convergence.

Solution

Solution. Once n2≥ϵ, the only way to have ∣Yn​∣≥ϵ is Yn​=n2, so P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)=n1​→0. In probability: yes.

The means: E[Yn​]=n2⋅n1​=n→∞, and more generally E[Ynr​]=n2r⋅n1​=n2r−1→∞ for every r≥1. So no Lr convergence for any r. (This is Bertsekas's answer to his Problem 7(b).) Same story as slide 21, just with an even bigger rare value.

B3 (last year's HW7 Q1; Bertsekas Problem 5). X1​,X2​,… independent U[−1,1]. Show convergence in probability, and find the limit, for: (a) Yn​=nXn​​; (b) Yn​=Xnn​; (c) Yn​=X1​X2​⋯Xn​; (d) Yn​=max{X1​,…,Xn​}.

Solution

Solution. (a) ∣Yn​∣≤n1​ always, so P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)=0 once n>ϵ1​. Limit 0.

(b) ∣Xn​∣ is uniform on [0,1] (fold [−1,1] in half). For 0<ϵ<1,

P(∣Xn​∣n≥ϵ)=P(∣Xn​∣≥ϵ1/n)=1−ϵ1/n→1−1=0,

since ϵ1/n→1. Limit 0. (A number in [0,1) raised to a huge power is tiny unless it's really close to 1, and that's increasingly unlikely.)

(c) A direct CDF is messy, so use Markov. By independence,

E∣Yn​∣=i=1∏n​E∣Xi​∣=(21​)n,

since E∣Xi​∣=21​. Then P(∣Yn​∣≥ϵ)≤ϵ2−n​→0. Limit 0.

(d) The max should creep up to 1. For 0<ϵ<2, ∣Yn​−1∣≥ϵ means Yn​≤1−ϵ (it can't exceed 1), i.e. all Xi​≤1−ϵ:

P(∣Yn​−1∣≥ϵ)=(2(1−ϵ)−(−1)​)n=(22−ϵ​)n→0.

Limit 1.

B4 (last year's HW7 Q2). Xi​ i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2>0. Let Yi​=31​Xi​+32​Xi+1​ and Mn​=n1​∑i=1n​Yi​. (a) Are the Yi​ independent? (b) Identically distributed? (c) Show Mn​p​μ.

Solution

Solution. (a) No. Yi​ and Yi+1​ both contain Xi+1​. Concretely, only the shared Xi+1​ contributes to the covariance:

Cov(Yi​,Yi+1​)=Cov(32​Xi+1​,31​Xi+1​)=92​σ2=0.

(b) Yes. Each Yi​ is the same function of an i.i.d. pair (Xi​,Xi+1​).

(c) We can't use the usual WLLN (not independent), but Chebyshev only needs the variance of Mn​ to go to 0. Mean: E[Yi​]=31​μ+32​μ=μ, so E[Mn​]=μ. Variance pieces:

  • Var(Yi​)=91​σ2+94​σ2=95​σ2,
  • neighbours: covariance 92​σ2, and there are n−1 neighbouring pairs, each counted twice,
  • non-neighbours share nothing, covariance 0.
Var(i=1∑n​Yi​)=n⋅95​σ2+2(n−1)⋅92​σ2=99n−4​σ2,Var(Mn​)=9n2(9n−4)σ2​≤nσ2​.

So Chebyshev gives P(∣Mn​−μ∣≥ϵ)≤nϵ2σ2​→0.

The lesson: the WLLN argument doesn't really need independence. It needs the variance of the average to go to 0, and weak dependence (only neighbours correlated) is fine.

B5 (last year's HW7 Q3 and HW8 Q5). (a) Xn​∼N(0,n1​): show Xn​p​0. (b) Xn​=X+Yn​ with Yn​∼N(0,n1​) independent of X: show Xn​m.s.​X.

Solution

Solution. (a) Mean 0, variance n1​, so Chebyshev: P(∣Xn​∣≥ϵ)≤nϵ21​→0. (b) The difference is just Yn​: E[(Xn​−X)2]=E[Yn2​]=n1​→0. We never needed to know anything about X.

B6 (last year's HW7 Q7). Xn​=X+Yn​ with E[Yn​]=n1​ and Var(Yn​)=nσ2​. Show Xn​p​X.

Solution

Solution. Again Xn​−X=Yn​. By bias–variance,

E[(Xn​−X)2]=E[Yn2​]=Var(Yn​)+(E[Yn​])2=nσ2​+n21​→0.

Mean square, so in probability too.

B7 (last year's Quiz 2 Q2; HW7 Q5; Tutorial 7 Q8(b)). Xn​ has the Laplace density 2n​e−n∣x∣. Show Xn​p​0.

Solution, three ways. (The density is symmetric, so double the right half.)

  • Directly: P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)=2∫ϵ∞​2n​e−nxdx=e−nϵ→0.
  • Markov: E∣Xn​∣=2∫0∞​x2n​e−nxdx=n⋅n21​=n1​, so P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤nϵ1​→0.
  • Chebyshev: E[Xn​]=0 by symmetry, and E[Xn2​]=2∫0∞​x22n​e−nxdx=n⋅n32​=n22​, so P(∣Xn​∣>ϵ)≤n2ϵ22​→0.

(The integrals use ∫0∞​xke−nxdx=nk+1k!​.) All three work. Notice how the exact answer e−nϵ is way smaller than both bounds.

B8 (last year's HW8 Q4; probabilitycourse 7.2.6; Tutorial 7 Q4(b); Endsem Q7). (a) Xn​∼U(0,n1​): show Xn​p​0 and Xn​Lr​0. (b) Endsem Q7: Xn​∼U(5−n1​,5+n1​): show Xn​d​5, and compute P(∣Xn​−5∣>ϵ) explicitly.

Solution

Solution. (a) Xn​ lives in (0,n1​), so P(Xn​>ϵ)=0 once n1​≤ϵ. And with density n on (0,n1​),

E[Xnr​]=∫01/n​xrndx=n⋅r+1(1/n)r+1​=(r+1)nr1​→0.

(b) In distribution. The limit is the constant 5, CDF 1{x≥5}, which jumps only at 5.

  • x<5: once 5−n1​>x, all of Xn​'s mass is to the right of x, so Fn​(x)=0. ✓
  • x>5: once 5+n1​<x, all the mass is to the left, so Fn​(x)=1. ✓
  • x=5: Fn​(5)=21​ for every n (5 is the midpoint). That's allowed to disagree with F(5)=1, since 5 is a jump point.

The probability. The density is 2n​ on an interval of half-width n1​ around 5.

  • If n1​≤ϵ: the whole interval is within ϵ of 5, so the probability is 0.
  • If n1​>ϵ: the part outside (5−ϵ,5+ϵ) is two pieces of length n1​−ϵ each, total 2(n1​−ϵ), times density 2n​:
P(∣Xn​−5∣>ϵ)={1−nϵ0​n<ϵ1​n≥ϵ1​​ n→∞​0.

B9 (last year's HW8 Q1). Independent Xn​∼ Bernoulli(n1​). Does Xn​→0 (a) in mean square, (b) almost surely, (c) in distribution?

Solution

Solution. (a) Yes. Xn2​=Xn​ (it's 0 or 1), so E[Xn2​]=n1​→0. (b) No. That's L17 Part B, B4 (Theorem 7.6, or second Borel–Cantelli). (c) Yes, because m.s. ⇒ p ⇒ d. Or directly: FXn​​(x)=0 for x<0, =1−n1​→1 for 0≤x<1, and =1 for x≥1. That's the CDF of the constant 0 in the limit. This is the standard "m.s. does not imply a.s." example.

B10 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q1). One uniform U and Xn​=n1{U≤n1​} (L17 slide 19). Does Xn​→0 in (a) distribution, (b) probability, (c) almost surely (can Borel–Cantelli be applied?), (d) mean?

Solution

Solution. Start with the strongest one. (c) Yes, almost surely (L17 slide 19). But Borel–Cantelli (Theorem 7.5) can't be used to show it, because ∑n​P(Xn​>ϵ)=∑n1​=∞. The conclusion holds anyway, by Theorem 7.6. (b), (a) Yes, both follow from (c). (d) No: E∣Xn​∣=n⋅n1​=1 for every n.

B11 (last year's Quiz 2, second set, Q1b): convergence in distribution only. Xn​∼ Exp(n) and Yn​=nXn​. Let Y∼ Exp(1), independent of all Yn​ (and the Yn​ independent). Does Yn​→Y in (a) distribution, (b) probability, (c) almost surely, (d) L1?

Solution

Solution. (a) Yes, and in the most boring way possible:

FYn​​(y)=P(Xn​≤ny​)=1−e−n⋅y/n=1−e−y.

Every Yn​ is exactly Exp(1), the same as Y.

(b) No. Yn​ and Y are independent Exp(1)s, so their difference doesn't shrink. Condition on Y=y:

P(Yn​>Y+ϵ)=∫0∞​P(Yn​>y+ϵ)e−ydy=∫0∞​e−(y+ϵ)e−ydy=21​e−ϵ,

and by symmetry the same for Y>Yn​+ϵ. So P(∣Yn​−Y∣>ϵ)=e−ϵ for every n, which doesn't go to 0.

(c) No, since a.s. would imply (b). (Or by Theorem 7.6: P(Am​)=∏n≥m​(1−e−ϵ)=0.)

(d) No. From (b), Yn​−Y has the Laplace density 21​e−∣z∣, so E∣Yn​−Y∣=1 for every n.

This is the cleanest exam-style example that d does not imply p: same distribution every time, but independent values that never get close.

B12 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q3). X∼ Bernoulli(31​) and Xn​=(1+n1​)X. Show Xn​p​X.

Solution

Solution. ∣Xn​−X∣=nX​≤n1​, so P(∣Xn​−X∣>ϵ)=0 once n>ϵ1​. (Even sure convergence.)

B13 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q10). Xi​ i.i.d. with E[X]=2 and Var(X)=9. Let Yi​=2iXi​​, Tn​=∑i=1n​Yi​ and An​=nTn​​. (a) Means and variances. (b) to (d) Do Yn​, Tn​, An​ converge in probability, and to what?

Solution

Solution. (a) Dividing by 2n divides the mean by 2n and the variance by 4n:

E[Yn​]=2n2​,Var(Yn​)=4n9​.

Sums of geometric series (independence for the variance):

E[Tn​]=2i=1∑n​2−i=2(1−2−n),Var(Tn​)=9i=1∑n​4−i=9⋅31−4−n​=3(1−4−n).

And dividing by n:

E[An​]=n2(1−2−n)​,Var(An​)=n23(1−4−n)​.

(b) Yn​→0: mean and variance both go to 0, so mean square, hence in probability.

(c) Tn​ does not go to a constant, because its variance goes to 3, not 0. Instead it converges (in mean square, hence in probability) to the random variable T=∑i=1∞​2iXi​​. Check: T−Tn​=∑i>n​Yi​, so

E[(T−Tn​)2]=Var(i>n∑​Yi​)+(Ei>n∑​Yi​)2=3⋅4−n+(2⋅2−n)2=7⋅4−n→0.

(d) An​→0: mean and variance go to 0. Careful, the limit is not E[X]=2. The Yi​ aren't identically distributed, so the LLN doesn't apply.

B14 (last year's HW8 Q11). Yi​ i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2, and Xn​=n1​(Y1​Y2​+Y2​Y3​+⋯+Yn−1​Yn​+Yn​Y1​). Show Xn​p​μ2.

Solution

Solution. Same plan as B4: mean, then a variance that goes to 0, then Chebyshev.

Mean. Each term is a product of two independent variables, mean μ⋅μ. So E[Xn​]=μ2.

Variance pieces. Let v=Var(Y1​Y2​). Since E[(Y1​Y2​)2]=E[Y2]2=(σ2+μ2)2, we get v=(σ2+μ2)2−μ4. Neighbouring products share one factor:

Cov(Y1​Y2​,Y2​Y3​)=E[Y1​Y22​Y3​]−μ4=μ2E[Y2]−μ4=μ2σ2.

Products with no common factor are independent, covariance 0.

For n≥3 the cyclic sum has n terms and n neighbouring pairs (it wraps around), each pair counted twice:

Var(Xn​)=n2nv+2nμ2σ2​=nv+2μ2σ2​→0.

Chebyshev finishes it.

B15 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q2): the "typewriter" sequence. U∼U[0,1]; X1​=1{U∈[0,1]}; X2​,X3​ are the indicators of the two halves; X4​,…,X7​ of the four quarters; and so on. Find the limit in probability, and decide almost sure convergence.

Solution

Solution. In the k-th sweep, the intervals have length 2−k. So for Xn​ in that sweep, P(Xn​=1)=2−k→0. Hence Xn​p​0, and in every Lr too, since E[Xnr​]=2−k→0.

But fix any u. Each sweep covers all of [0,1], so in every sweep exactly one of the indicators equals 1 at u. That's infinitely many 1s on every path. No path converges, so Xn​→0 almost surely.

Another "m.s. does not imply a.s." example, and this one has no independence at all. A narrower and narrower "window" keeps sweeping across [0,1] and hits every point again and again.

B16 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q4). Show μ^​n​→E[X] in mean square.

Solution

Solution. E[(μ^​n​−μ)2]=Var(μ^​n​)=nσ2​→0.

Convergence in distribution

B17 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q2). Xi​ i.i.d. U[0,1] and Yn​=n(1−maxi≤n​Xi​). Show Yn​d​ Exp(1).

Solution

Solution. The gap between the max and 1 is about n1​, so scaling by n should give something nontrivial. Use the max trick:

P(Yn​>y)=P(maxXi​<1−ny​)=(1−ny​)n→e−y(0≤y<n).

So FYn​​(y)→1−e−y for y≥0, and both CDFs are 0 for y<0. That's Exp(1).

B18 (last year's Tutorial 7 Q4(a) and Tutorial 8 Q5): discrete to continuous. Yn​ uniform on {1,…,n} and Xn​=nYn​​. Show Xn​d​U(0,1).

Solution

Solution. Xn​ is uniform on the grid {n1​,n2​,…,1}, which gets finer and finer. For 0≤x≤1,

FXn​​(x)=P(Yn​≤nx)=n⌊nx⌋​.

Since nx−1<⌊nx⌋≤nx, we get x−n1​<FXn​​(x)≤x, so FXn​​(x)→x. Outside [0,1] both CDFs are 0 or 1. So discrete variables can converge in distribution to a continuous one.

B19 (probabilitycourse 7.2.8, Problem 1). Xn​∼ Geometric(nλ​) and Yn​=nXn​​. Show Yn​d​ Exp(λ).

Solution

Solution. For a geometric, P(X>m)=(1−p)m (the first m trials all fail). So

P(Yn​>y)=P(Xn​>ny)=(1−nλ​)⌊ny⌋.

Write ⌊ny⌋=ny−θ with 0≤θ<1. Then (1−nλ​)ny→e−λy, and (1−nλ​)−θ→1. So P(Yn​>y)→e−λy, the Exp(λ) tail.

This is the continuous cousin of Binomial → Poisson: the waiting time over lots of tiny trials becomes exponential.

B20 (last year's HW8 Q9): hypergeometric to binomial. A bag has n blue and n red balls; draw 10 without replacement; Xn​ is the number of blue balls. Show Xn​d​ Binomial(10,21​).

Solution

Solution. For k=0,…,10, write out the hypergeometric pmf and pull out the (k10​):

P(Xn​=k)=(102n​)(kn​)(10−kn​)​=(k10​)10 factors2n(2n−1)⋯(2n−9)​​n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)​k factors​⋅n(n−1)⋯(n−9+k)​10−k factors​​.

The top has 10 factors each ≈n, the bottom has 10 factors each ≈2n. So

P(Xn​=k)⟶(k10​)(2n)10n10​=(k10​)2101​.

By Theorem 7.1 that's convergence in distribution. With a huge bag, removing 10 balls barely changes the proportions, so without replacement is basically with replacement.

B21 (last year's HW8 Q6). Xn​=n​Z​ with E[Z2]<∞. Show Xn​d​0.

Solution

Solution. E[Xn2​]=nE[Z2]​→0. Mean square ⇒ in probability ⇒ in distribution.

Normal approximation (CLT)

For all of these, follow the slide 30 recipe: identify μ and σ2 per term, scale up to the sum or average, standardise, look up Φ.

B22 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.9). 100 packages with weights i.i.d. U[5,50] pounds. P(total>3000)?

Solution

Solution. One package: μ=25+50​=27.5, σ2=12(50−5)2​=168.75. Total of 100: mean 2750, variance 16875, SD ≈129.9.

z=129.93000−2750​=1.92,P≈1−Φ(1.92)=0.027.

B23 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.10): turning a count into a sum. Processing times are i.i.d. U[1,5]. Find P(at least 100 parts processed within 320 time units).

Solution

Solution. The number of parts done isn't a sum of i.i.d. things, but there's a trick: "at least 100 parts done by time 320" is the same event as "the first 100 parts took at most 320 in total", i.e. {S100​≤320}. Now it's a sum.

One part: μ=3, σ2=12(5−1)2​=34​. Sum of 100: mean 300, SD 400/3​=11.55.

z=11.55320−300​=1.73,P≈Φ(1.73)=0.958.

B24 (Bertsekas Ex. 5.11): Bertsekas 5.5 again, with the CLT. Mn​ is the average of n i.i.d. Bernoulli(p). Var(Mn​)=np(1−p)​≤4n1​, so σMn​​≤2n​1​ and

P(∣Mn​−p∣≥ϵ)≈2(1−Φ(σMn​​ϵ​))≤2(1−Φ(2ϵn​)).

(Bigger σ means a bigger probability, so the worst case σ=2n​1​ gives an upper bound.)

(a) n=100, ϵ=0.1: ≤2(1−Φ(2))=0.0455. Chebyshev only gave 0.25. (b) Within 0.01 with probability 0.95: need 2(1−Φ(0.02n​))≤0.05, i.e. 0.02n​≥1.96, so n≥9604. Compare Chebyshev's 50,000.

B25 (last year's HW8 Q2). Call durations have μ=10 and σ=10 minutes. (a) For 50 calls, P(Xˉ>12). (b) Minimum n with P(Xˉ>12)≤0.05. (c) For 80 calls, P(9<Xˉ<11). (Given: Φ−1(0.95)=1.6449, Φ(2​)=0.9214, Φ(0.8944)=0.8147.)

Solution

Solution. Here everything is about the average, with SD(Xˉ)=n​10​. (a) z=10/50​12−10​=10250​​=2​, so P≈1−0.9214=0.0786. (b) Need 1−Φ(102n​​)≤0.05, i.e. 102n​​≥1.6449. So n​≥8.22, n≥67.6, and the answer is n=68. (c) z=10/80​1​=0.8944 on each side, so P≈Φ(0.8944)−Φ(−0.8944)=2(0.8147)−1=0.6294.

B26 (last year's HW8 Q3). Rods: μ=100 mm, σ=5 mm, roughly normal. (a) P(one rod>110). (b) P(mean of 36>103).

Solution

Solution. (a) z=5110−100​=2, so 1−0.9772=0.0228. (b) SD(Xˉ)=36​5​=65​, so z=5/63​=3.6 and P≈1−0.9998=0.0002. Being 3 above the mean is fairly common for one rod, but super rare for an average of 36. Averages vary a lot less than individual values.

B27 (last year's HW8 Q8 = Bertsekas Problem 8; Tutorial 8 Q8). (a) A fair roulette (odd with probability 21​) is watched for 100 rounds; you call it unfair if more than 55 are odd. P(wrong decision)? (b) P(>220 heads in 400 tosses). Are (a) and (b) the same? (c) P(40≤ heads ≤60) in 100 tosses.

Solution

Solution. (a) The wheel is fair, so a wrong decision means S>55 with S∼ Binomial(100,21​): mean 50, SD 5. "More than 55" is S≥56, so the corrected boundary is 55.5:

P≈1−Φ(555.5−50​)=1−Φ(1.1)=0.1357.

(Exact 0.1356. Without the correction you'd get 1−Φ(1)=0.159.)

(b) Mean 200, SD 10. "More than 220" is ≥221, boundary 220.5:

1−Φ(10220.5−200​)=1−Φ(2.05)=0.0202(exact 0.0201).

Not the same, even though 55% of 100 and 55% of 400 look like the same thing. The SD of the proportion is n​0.5​, which halves when n quadruples. So the same excess proportion is twice as many SDs away. More data makes the same deviation less likely. That's the LLN showing up.

(c) P(40≤S≤60)≈P(39.5≤normal≤60.5)=2Φ(2.1)−1=0.9643 (exact 0.9648).

B28 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q6). Test scores: mean 75, SD 10, roughly normal. (a) P(score≥100). (b) Out of 100 people, how many expected below 60? (c) P(mean of 100<70).

Solution

Solution. (a) z=2.5: 1−Φ(2.5)=0.0062. (b) P(below 60)=Φ(−1.5)=0.0668, so the expected count is 100×0.0668≈6.7 (linearity of expectation over 100 indicators). (c) SD(Xˉ)=100​10​=1, so z=−5: Φ(−5)≈2.9×10−7. Basically impossible.

B29 (last year's Tutorial 8 Q9; probabilitycourse 7.1.2). Service times: mean 2, variance 1, independent. Y = total for 50 customers. P(90<Y<110)?

Solution

Solution. E[Y]=100, SD(Y)=50​. Symmetric interval of half-width 10:

P≈Φ(50​10​)−Φ(−50​10​)=2Φ(2​)−1=0.8427.

B30 (probabilitycourse 7.1.3, Problems 1 to 4).

  1. 100 passengers, weight mean 170 and SD 30 lb. P(total>18,000). Total: mean 17,000, SD 30100​=300. z=3001000​=310​, so 1−Φ(3.33)≈4.3×10−4.

  2. ±1 steps. Xi​=+1 w.p. 0.6 and −1 w.p. 0.4; Y=X1​+⋯+X25​; estimate P(4≤Y≤6) with a continuity correction. Per step, E[Xi​]=0.6−0.4=0.2 and Var(Xi​)=E[Xi2​]−0.04=1−0.04=0.96. So E[Y]=5 and Var(Y)=24. The source's answer uses [3.5,6.5]: 2Φ(24​1.5​)−1=0.2405. But watch out. A sum of 25 terms each ±1 is always odd (25 odd numbers add to an odd number). So {4≤Y≤6}={Y=5}, which needs 15 ups and 10 downs, with exact probability (1525​)0.6150.410=0.161. The values of Y are 2 apart, not 1, so the right correction is half the step, ±1: P≈2Φ(24​1​)−1=0.162, almost exact. The ±21​ rule assumes values 1 apart.

  3. 64 guests each want 0, 1, 2 sandwiches w.p. 41​,21​,41​. How many to make so all are served with probability 0.95? Per guest: mean 1, variance E[X2]−1=21​+1−1=21​. Total: mean 64, SD 32​=42​≈5.66. Need c with Φ(5.66c−64​)≥0.95: c≥64+1.6449×5.66=73.3. So make 74.

  4. Sample size. Xi​∼ Exp(1) (mean 1, SD 1); smallest n with P(0.9≤Xˉ≤1.1)≥0.95. SD(Xˉ)=n​1​, so we need 2Φ(0.1n​)−1≥0.95, i.e. 0.1n​≥1.96, n≥384.2, so n=385.

B31 (Bertsekas Problem 9): normal vs Poisson approximation. Each day the computer crashes with probability 0.05, independently. Find P(at least 45 crash-free days out of 50) (a) by the normal approximation, (b) by the Poisson approximation.

Solution

Solution. Flip it around: let X∼ Binomial(50,0.05) count the crash days. At least 45 crash-free means X≤5. Mean np=2.5, variance np(1−p)=2.375. (a) Φ(2.375​5.5−2.5​)=Φ(1.95)=0.974. (b) Poisson(2.5): ∑k=05​e−2.5k!2.5k​=0.958. The exact answer is 0.962, so Poisson wins. That makes sense: p is small and np is moderate, which is Poisson's home turf, while the binomial is too skewed for the normal to fit well.

B32 (Bertsekas Problem 10). Daily gadget counts are i.i.d. with mean 5 and variance 9. (a) P(total in 100 days<440). (b) Largest n with P(X1​+⋯+Xn​≥200+5n)≤0.05. (c) N = first day the total exceeds 1000. Approximate P(N≥220).

Solution

Solution. (a) Total over 100 days: mean 500, SD 3⋅10=30. Φ(30440−500​)=Φ(−2)=0.023. (b) Sn​ has mean 5n and SD 3n​, so the event is "Sn​ at least 200 above its mean":

P≈1−Φ(3n​200​)≤0.05⟺3n​200​≥1.645⟺n​≤40.5⟺n≤1642.

(c) Same trick as B23. N≥220 means the total hadn't passed 1000 by day 219: {S219​≤1000}. Mean 1095, SD 3219​=44.4:

P≈Φ(44.41000−1095​)=Φ(−2.14)=0.016.

B33 (Bertsekas Problem 11). Xi​,Yi​ i.i.d. U[0,1] and W=16(X1​+⋯+X16​)−(Y1​+⋯+Y16​)​. Approximate P(∣W−E[W]∣<0.001).

Solution

Solution. E[W]=0. W is a combination of 32 independent uniforms, each with variance 121​ (the minus sign doesn't change the variance):

Var(W)=16232⋅121​​=961​,SD(W)=0.102.
P≈2Φ(0.1020.001​)−1=2Φ(0.0098)−1≈0.0078.

Tiny, because the window ±0.001 is only about a hundredth of an SD wide.

B34 (last year's HW8 Q12, bonus): binomial to normal without MGFs (sketch). Write P(k)=(kN​)pkqN−k, take logs, and use Stirling, lnN!≈NlnN−N. Put k=Np+x and expand lnP(k) to second order in x around the peak k=Np.

  • The first-order term vanishes. That's exactly why the peak is at Np.
  • The second-order coefficient comes out as −2Npq1​.

So P(k)≈Ce−x2/(2Npq): a Gaussian shape with mean Np and variance Npq. Normalising fixes C=2πNpq​1​. (The sharper Stirling formula N!≈2πN​(N/e)N gives the constant directly.)
